```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Lag sequential analysis counts transitions between consecutive events of
the same sequence. What counts as a sequence therefore decides what counts
as a transition: two actions by different students are not a transition,
and neither are the last action of one working session and the first action
of the next one a day later. With data that arrive as an event log, one row
per recorded action, the analysis starts by recovering the sequences: which
rows belong together, in what order, and where a sequence ends.

`lsa()` performs that step itself. It accepts wide sequence data, a long
event log described by a small set of column arguments, and the sequence
objects of the `tna` and `Nestimate` packages, and it returns a fit whose
transition probabilities, initial probabilities, and network can be handed
back to those packages. This guide covers each input form, the rules that
split a log into sequences, grouped logs, and the export of a fit. The
column grammar is the one used by `tna::prepare_data()` and
`Nestimate::build_network()`, so a log prepared for one of them needs no
change.

```{r package}
library(lagdynamics)
```

## Data

Three bundled data sets cover the input forms.

- `group_regulation_long`: an event log of collaborative learning, 27,533
  rows. **Actor:** `Actor` (2,000 students). **Action:** `Action`, nine
  regulation codes. **Time:** `Time`, a POSIXct time stamp. **Group:**
  `Achiever` (`High` or `Low`), fixed for each actor.
- `ai_long`: an event log of coded AI behaviours in human-AI programming
  sessions, 8,551 rows. **Actor:** `project` (34 projects). **Session:**
  `session_id` (428 sessions). **Action:** `code`, eight behaviour codes.
  **Order:** `order_in_session`, the position of the coded message within
  its session.
- `group_regulation` and `engagement`: wide data, one row per sequence and
  one column per time point.

```{r data}
head(group_regulation_long)
head(ai_long)
```

## Wide sequence data

Wide data need no column arguments: each row is a sequence and the columns
are read in order. `group_regulation` holds the same 2,000 sequences as the
long log above, already assembled.

```{r wide}
fit_wide <- lsa(group_regulation)
as.data.frame(summary(fit_wide))
```

The wide data give 2,000 sequences with 25,533 transitions among nine
states. Sequences differ in length, and the missing cells that pad the
shorter rows are dropped, so no transition is counted into or out of them.

## Long event logs

A long log is described by naming its columns, as strings:

| Argument | Role |
|---|---|
| `action` | The state of each event. Required; naming it switches to long-format input. |
| `actor` | Who produced the event. Each actor's events form a sequence. |
| `session` | A working session. Each session, or each actor-session pair when both are given, forms a sequence. |
| `time` | A time stamp that orders the events (POSIXct, a parseable string, or Unix time with `is_unix_time = TRUE`). |
| `order` | An explicit position that orders the events; used in preference to `time`. |
| `group` | A grouping column, fixed within each sequence, for one model per group. |

The regulation log has an actor, an action, and a time stamp.

```{r long}
fit_long <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
                time = "Time")
as.data.frame(summary(fit_long))
```

The log is assembled into 2,000 sequences, one per actor, with the same
25,533 transitions as the wide data. The two fits are the same model:

```{r long-equals-wide}
isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_long), transitions(fit_wide),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
```

## Where a sequence ends

When `time` is given without `session`, a sequence also ends wherever two
consecutive events of an actor are more than `time_threshold` seconds apart,
900 seconds (15 minutes) by default. The threshold is an analytic choice: it
states how long a pause has to be before the next action no longer counts as
a response to the previous one. A shorter threshold splits the same log into
more, shorter sequences.

```{r threshold}
fit_5min <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
                time = "Time", time_threshold = 300)
as.data.frame(summary(fit_5min))
```

With a five-minute threshold the 2,000 actor logs break into 12,305
sequences, and the number of transitions falls from 25,533 to 15,228: every
pause longer than five minutes removes the transition that spanned it. The
independence test remains decisive (G² = 7,927 on 64 degrees of freedom) and
69 transitions stay significant, against 72 with the default, so the
structure of the process does not hinge on the threshold. Comparing the fit
at two thresholds in this way is the sensitivity check the choice needs.

Without `actor` or `session`, the whole log is one stream ordered by `time`.
The regulation log interleaves 2,000 students working at the same time, so
a single stream mixes their actions into transitions that never happened:

```{r one-stream}
fit_stream <- lsa(group_regulation_long, action = "Action", time = "Time")
as.data.frame(summary(fit_stream))
```

The stream gives one sequence of 27,532 transitions, and its independence
test is not significant (G² = 46.2, df = 64, p = 0.954): interleaving the
students destroys the sequential structure. The `actor` argument is what
makes the regulation log analysable.

## Sessions and explicit order

The AI log records sessions within projects and an explicit position of each
coded message within its session. Naming `actor` and `session` makes each
project-session pair a sequence, and `order` sets the order of events within
it. Several codes can share a message, and the position column keeps them in
the order they were coded.

```{r session}
fit_ai <- lsa(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
              action = "code", order = "order_in_session")
fit_ai
```

The log yields 428 sequences, one per session, with 8,123 transitions among
eight codes. Forty of the 64 transitions depart from chance, and the
strongest favoured transition is `Investigate -> Plan` (z = 33.4). Most sessions open with
`Investigate` (initial probability 0.715).

## Large logs: the actor-session key

When both `actor` and `session` are given, the sequence key is built over the
full cross of distinct actors and distinct sessions. The size of that cross
is held in an R integer, so once the number of distinct actors times the
number of distinct sessions passes 2,147,483,647, the largest
integer R can hold, the key overflows. The affected events lose their
sequence and are dropped, and the only sign is an "NAs produced by integer
overflow" warning. A log of 50,000 actors and 50,000 sessions is enough to
trigger it.

On a large log, compare the number of sequences in the summary with the
number of distinct sessions. When the session identifiers are already unique
across actors, as in `ai_long`, pass the session column as `actor` and omit
`session`; the key is then built over the sessions alone.

```{r session-as-actor}
fit_ai_sessions <- lsa(ai_long, actor = "session_id", action = "code",
                       order = "order_in_session")
as.data.frame(summary(fit_ai_sessions))
isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_ai_sessions), transitions(fit_ai),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
```

Keying on the session alone recovers the same 428 sequences and an identical
transition table, so the two calls are interchangeable here, and only the
second one is safe on a log too large for the cross.

## Grouped long logs

Adding `group` fits one model per group from the same log, under one shared
set of states. The grouping column must take a single value within each
recovered sequence; a sequence that spans two groups is an error.

```{r grouped}
gfit <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
            time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
gfit
summary(gfit)
```

The high and the low achievers contribute 1,000 sequences each, with 12,721
and 12,812 transitions. Every reading verb on a grouped fit returns a
leading `group` column, and the grouped fit is the input of the group
comparisons covered in [the group-comparison vignette](group-comparison.html).

```{r grouped-read}
transitions(gfit, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(4)
```

## tna objects

A `tna` model keeps the sequences it was fitted from, and `lsa()` reads them
directly. The model below is fitted by `tna` to the wide `engagement` data
and passed to `lsa()`.

```{r tna-in}
tna_fit <- tna::tna(engagement)
tna_fit
fit_from_tna <- lsa(tna_fit)
isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_from_tna), transitions(lsa(engagement)),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
```

Loading `tna` prints a notice that it registers its own plot method for
bootstrap results in place of the one from `cograph`; the notice does not
concern the models. The fit from the `tna` model and the fit from the
original data are identical. The same holds for the output of `tna::prepare_data()`, which
`lsa()` accepts as it stands. A grouped `tna` model (`group_tna`) is read
as well, but its groups are pooled into a single fit; for one model per
group, fit the log with `group =` as in the previous section.

## Nestimate objects

`Nestimate::build_network()` uses the same long-log grammar and keeps the
prepared sequences in the network object, which `lsa()` reads.

```{r nestimate-in}
net <- Nestimate::build_network(ai_long, method = "tna", actor = "project",
                                session = "session_id", action = "code",
                                order = "order_in_session")
fit_from_nestimate <- lsa(net)
isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_from_nestimate), transitions(fit_ai),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
```

`Nestimate` reports that two metadata columns (`session_date` and
`cluster`) vary within some sessions and keeps their first value; the
message concerns those columns only, not the sequences. The `Nestimate`
network and the direct `lsa()` call on the log recover the same transition
table.

## From a fit to tna and other tools

A fit exposes the quantities that transition network tools consume.
`transition_probabilities()` returns the row-stochastic transition matrix as
a tidy data frame, one row per `from -> to` pair, and `initial()` the
distribution of first states.

```{r probabilities}
transition_probabilities(fit_long) |> head(9)
initial(fit_long)
```

The nine rows shown are the transitions out of `adapt`; their probabilities
sum to one. The most common first states are `consensus` (0.2140) and
`plan` (0.2045).
For a grouped fit both tables carry a leading `group` column.

`lsa_to_tna()` converts a fit to a `tna` model, so the `tna` toolkit
(centralities, communities, cliques, its plots) applies to a model estimated
here. `weights` chooses the edge weights; `"prob"` gives the transition
probabilities of a standard transition network.

```{r to-tna}
tn <- lsa_to_tna(fit_from_tna, weights = "prob")
tna::centralities(tn, measures = c("InStrength", "OutStrength", "Betweenness"))
```

`Average` receives the most probability from the other states
(in-strength 0.664) and is the only state that lies on shortest paths
between the other two (betweenness 2, against 0 for `Active` and
`Disengaged`). A grouped fit converts to a `group_tna` model, one
`tna` model per group:

```{r to-group-tna}
tna::centralities(lsa_to_tna(gfit), measures = "InStrength")
```

`consensus` is the state with the most incoming probability in both groups,
with in-strength 2.95 among the high achievers and 2.42 among the low
achievers.

A fit is also a `cograph_network`, so it can be drawn directly as a
transition network with probability weights; the displays are covered in
[the plotting guide](plotting.html).

## Summary

| Input | Call |
|---|---|
| Wide data, one row per sequence | `lsa(data)` |
| Long log, one sequence per actor | `lsa(log, actor = , action = , time = )` |
| Long log with sessions and explicit order | `lsa(log, actor = , session = , action = , order = )` |
| Very large log with globally unique sessions | `lsa(log, actor = "<session column>", action = , order = )` |
| One model per group | add `group = ` |
| `tna` model, `tna::prepare_data()` output | `lsa(object)` |
| `Nestimate` network or prepared data | `lsa(object)` |
| Hand a fit to `tna` | `lsa_to_tna(fit)` |
| Transition and initial probabilities as tables | `transition_probabilities(fit)`, `initial(fit)` |

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
